data.sample_text:
OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

Important

This repository is maintained as a legacy entry point and historical archive. Active development has moved to GenAI-Security-Project/GenAI-LLM-Top10.

Current release: OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 — published August 4, 2026.

Get the 2026 publication · Browse the current source · Report a correction

  

About This Repository

This repository powered the original OWASP project page and contains historical releases, translations, working files, and supporting materials for the OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications.

It remains available so existing links, citations, and historical artifacts continue to work. New issues, pull requests, and release work should be directed to the active repository.

The Top 10 is now a core initiative within the broader OWASP GenAI Security Project, which develops freely available guidance and resources for securing generative AI systems and applications.

Releases
OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 — current release
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 — archived release
Earlier releases and translations — historical material
Contributing

Use the active repository to:

Report a correction to the 2026 release
Submit broader release feedback
Open a pull request

For the broader project contribution process, visit genai.owasp.org/contribute.

We have a working group channel on OWASP Slack: #team-genai-top-10-llm.

arxiv_papers.summary: We ask what AI coding agents and AI security harnesses find that deterministic static application security testing (SAST) does not, and what they miss that SAST catches. VulnBench 2.0 is a benchmark of 108 hand-curated, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in 20 open-source web applications in Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python and Java; 62 flow across more than one file. arxiv_papers.title: What Victims Take Away: Attack Reuse and Defense Revision after Prompt-Injection Attacks
arxiv_papers.summary: Attack logs and red-team reports show targets the attacks used against them, to help them repair their defenses. Prompt injections against large language models (LLMs) are plain text, so such records also hand targets a working copy. arxiv_papers.title: Bringing Hardware Security Education to All: A Seamless Curriculum Integration Approach
arxiv_papers.summary: Cybersecurity education has predominantly focused on software and network security, under the assumption that the underlying hardware is trustworthy. Threats introduced through the global semiconductor supply chain, together with vulnerabilities arising during design and integration, challenge the assumption that hardware can serve as an unquestioned root of trust. arxiv_papers.summary: Most graph-based Anti-Money Laundering (AML) methods assume access to a pooled transaction graph containing all accounts and payments, which in reality does not exist. Federated learning offers the necessary privacy guarantees but it remains unclear how money laundering patterns spanning separate graphs can effectively be detected. arxiv_papers.title: Can Open Be Too Open? On the Security and Trustworthiness of Fully Transparent LLMs
arxiv_papers.summary: There are different levels of transparency for LLMs: open weights, open data, and/or open pipeline. Recently, more interest has emerged in fully transparent LLMs, i.e., LLMs with fully open weights, data, and training pipeline. arxiv_papers.title: AI Security Literacy: Ecosystem-based Competency Framework and K-12 Learning Platform
arxiv_papers.summary: Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. arxiv_papers.title: Fake News, Real Crashes: Information Injection Attacks on LLM Financial Trading Agents
arxiv_papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now trade real capital using news as evidence, yet they cannot reliably tell fabricated headlines from real news. Because they read the same feeds under near-identical policies, a single fabricated post can push them into the same trade at the same moment.
